title: ASP.NET Core and EF Core
blurb: DI lifetimes, the middleware pipeline, model binding, configuration, EF Core. The two most reliably asked .NET interview questions live in here.

questions.q: What is the difference between Singleton, Scoped and Transient?
choices: Singleton: one per request. Scoped: one per application. Transient: one per calling thread
Singleton: one for the app's lifetime. Scoped: one per request. Transient: new on each resolve
They set thread safety: Singleton is locked, Scoped is per thread, Transient is unsynchronised
They set GC behaviour: Singleton is never collected, Scoped and Transient are collected early
questions.why: Lifetimes decide how many instances the container creates, not how they are locked or collected. DbContext is scoped because it tracks changes for one unit of work. Stateless helpers can be singletons, which must then be thread-safe on their own. Transient suits cheap objects with no shared state.
questions.asked: The single most asked .NET interview question. Know it cold.

questions.q: What is a captive dependency?
choices: Two services that depend on each other, so the container can never finish building either
A service registered twice with different lifetimes, so the last registration silently wins
A longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one, such as a singleton capturing a DbContext
A dependency created with `new` inside a service, so the container cannot manage its lifetime
questions.why: In Development, scope validation is on and the host throws at startup ("Cannot consume scoped service from singleton"). In Production validation is off by default, so the scoped object is silently captured on first resolution and shared by every request, which is neither thread-safe nor correct. Inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work.
questions.asked: The natural depth follow-up to the lifetimes question, and it separates real experience from memorisation.

questions.q: Why does the order of `app.Use...` calls matter?
choices: It does not: ASP.NET Core sorts the built-in middleware into a safe order at startup
Middleware forms an ordered pipeline; each one can short-circuit or pass to the next
Only the first and last calls matter, because the middle ones run in parallel
Order matters only for authentication; every other middleware can go anywhere
questions.why: Each middleware wraps the ones registered after it. UseAuthentication must come before UseAuthorization, both before the endpoints, and UseCors before anything that would short-circuit a preflight. Nothing re-sorts them for you, and a wrong order usually fails silently rather than crashing.
questions.asked: The second most asked .NET question. Expect to be asked to place a few in order.

questions.q: How does a middleware short-circuit the pipeline?
choices: By throwing an OperationCanceledException, which stops the pipeline cleanly
By returning false from InvokeAsync, which tells the host to stop there
By writing a response and not calling `await next(context)`
By calling `context.Abort()`, which completes the request normally
questions.why: Not calling `next` means nothing later in the pipeline runs. That is how authorisation returns 401 without reaching your endpoint and how caching serves a hit. `Abort()` resets the connection rather than sending a response, and a thrown exception becomes an error. Calling next after writing the response is a common bug: the headers are already sent.
questions.asked: Tests whether you could write a middleware yourself, not only configure the built-in ones.

questions.q: With the default WebApplication builder, where is configuration read from, and in what order?
choices: Environment variables, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, then appsettings.json; first found wins
appsettings.json only, unless you call AddEnvironmentVariables yourself, and then variables win
appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development only), env vars, CLI
Command line, then environment variables, then the JSON files; a key set earlier cannot change
questions.why: Later providers override earlier ones, which is what lets a container override a file value with an environment variable, and the command line override both. User secrets are added only in Development. The default builder already adds environment variables. Nested keys use `Section__Key` in environment variables.
questions.asked: Explains "why is production using the wrong connection string", which is a real debugging question.

questions.q: What is the difference between `IOptions<T>`, `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` and `IOptionsMonitor<T>`?
choices: IOptions re-reads on each access; IOptionsSnapshot caches for the app's life; IOptionsMonitor is for logs
IOptions is a singleton read once; IOptionsSnapshot is re-read per request; IOptionsMonitor notifies changes
IOptions is for secrets; IOptionsSnapshot is for appsettings.json; IOptionsMonitor is for environment variables
All three behave the same at runtime; they differ only in the package and namespace they come from
questions.why: If a config change should take effect without a restart, IOptions will not see it. IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, so it cannot be injected into a singleton (a captive dependency); IOptionsMonitor is a singleton with `CurrentValue` and `OnChange`, which is the one to use there. None of them is tied to a configuration source.
questions.asked: A standard mid-level .NET question; the singleton follow-up shows whether you have used it.

questions.q: In a controller marked `[ApiController]`, what happens when the request body fails validation?
choices: Nothing automatic: the action must check ModelState.IsValid itself before using the input
The model binder throws, and the developer exception page shows the validation errors
An automatic 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body is returned before the action runs
The invalid fields are reset to defaults and the action runs as if the input were valid
questions.why: `[ApiController]` adds a filter that short-circuits invalid model state with a 400 and a ValidationProblemDetails body. Without the attribute, or in a minimal API without the opt-in validation added in .NET 10, you check yourself, which is what the first choice describes. Knowing which applies is what the question is testing.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know what the framework does for you and where it stops.

questions.q: What is model binding?
choices: Binding a Razor view to a model so that edits in the view update the model object
Mapping an entity class to a database table, including its columns and relations
Serialising the action's return value into JSON in the format the client asked for
Mapping route values, query string, headers and body onto action parameters
questions.why: The bug it causes: a complex type binds from the body by default, a simple type from the route or query. Getting a null parameter usually means the value was not where the binder looked, hence `[FromBody]`, `[FromQuery]` and friends. Table mapping is EF Core, and writing the response is output formatting.
questions.asked: Definitional, but the null-parameter bug is the practical follow-up.

questions.q: What is ProblemDetails?
choices: A structured logging format that records the exception type, message and stack trace
The standard error body from RFC 9457 (formerly 7807): type, title, status, detail
The base exception class that ASP.NET Core maps to HTTP status codes for you
The JSON body a health check endpoint returns when a dependency is unhealthy
questions.why: Using the standard shape means clients and tooling can parse errors without bespoke code. `AddProblemDetails()` plus the exception handler middleware produce it for unhandled errors, rather than a try/catch in every action. It is a response format, not an exception type or a log format.
questions.asked: Shows you design consistent error responses instead of ad-hoc strings.

questions.q: What does EF Core's change tracker do?
choices: Logs every query the context runs, so that data access can be audited later
Caches query results between requests, so repeated reads skip the database
Records which migrations have been applied, so the schema always matches the model
Records original values of loaded entities, so SaveChanges can write UPDATEs
questions.why: It is why you can change a loaded entity and call SaveChanges with no explicit update: EF compares current values with the snapshot. It does not cache across requests (each context is short-lived), and migrations history lives in a table. For read-only queries `AsNoTracking()` skips the bookkeeping.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always AsNoTracking, an easy, concrete performance win to mention.

questions.q: What typically causes an N+1 query pattern in EF Core?
choices: Reading a navigation property with default settings, which loads it once per row
Calling SaveChanges in a loop, which re-runs the original query for each entity
Lazy-loading proxies being enabled, or a query issued inside a loop over results
Registering the DbContext as transient, so each entity gets its own query
questions.why: Lazy loading is off by default in EF Core: with default settings an unloaded navigation is just null (a NullReferenceException, not N+1). The extra queries appear when proxies are switched on, or when your code queries inside a loop. Fix it with `Include`, a `Select` projection or a split query, and log the generated SQL in development to see it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know EF Core defaults, not only the N+1 definition.

questions.q: Why is DbContext registered as Scoped?
choices: It is expensive to construct, so one per request is the cheapest safe option
It is not thread-safe and represents one unit of work, so one per request fits
It keeps its database connection open for the whole request to avoid reconnecting
EF Core migrations require it and fail at design time for other lifetimes
questions.why: Two concurrent requests sharing a context would corrupt the change tracker. Construction is cheap (and `AddDbContextPool` reuses instances when it matters), and connections are opened per operation and pooled by ADO.NET. For background work you create your own scope or context rather than borrowing the request's.
questions.asked: Connects DI lifetimes to a concrete type; the background-work follow-up is common.

questions.q: What is a migration in EF Core?
choices: A generated C# class describing a schema change, checked in and applied in order
A data import script that copies rows from one environment's database to another
A change to the model classes that EF applies to the database on the next start
A snapshot backup of the database taken before a deploy, used for rolling back
questions.why: `dotnet ef migrations add` scaffolds it from model changes and `database update` applies it. Model changes alone do nothing to the database until a migration is generated and applied. In production, migrating at startup is convenient and risky: a failed migration takes the app down and multiple instances race.
questions.asked: Basic EF workflow; the production-apply follow-up is where experience shows.

questions.q: What is the difference between a minimal API and a controller-based API?
choices: Minimal APIs cannot use dependency injection, so they suit only stateless endpoints
Controllers are deprecated since .NET 8 and remain only for backwards compatibility
Minimal APIs cannot return JSON directly and need a controller to serialise it
Minimal APIs map handlers directly; controllers add conventions and filters
questions.why: Both are first-class and share routing, DI, auth and model binding. Minimal APIs suit small services and read quickly; controllers earn their keep on large surfaces with cross-cutting filters and conventions. Minimal API handlers take services as parameters and return JSON by default.
questions.asked: Checks you are current; "controllers are legacy" and "minimal APIs are toys" are both wrong.

questions.q: How should long-running work triggered by a request be handled?
choices: Await it in the action, and raise the server's request timeout far enough to cover it
Start it with async void so the request returns while the work continues
Run it on a new Thread so it outlives the request and its pipeline
Queue it, return 202 Accepted with a status URL, and process it in the background
questions.why: Holding a request open ties up resources, hits proxy timeouts and dies with the deploy. A hosted service reading from a durable queue survives restarts. Async void and raw threads are fire-and-forget: their failures go unobserved and the work is lost when the process stops.
questions.asked: A design question disguised as a .NET one; the strong answer mentions durability.

questions.q: What does `IHostedService` / `BackgroundService` give you?
choices: A cron-style scheduler that runs a job once across all instances at a set time
A long-running task with startup and graceful-shutdown hooks tied to the host
A durable message queue that keeps pending work safe across process restarts
Automatic retries with exponential backoff for work that fails transiently
questions.why: It gets a CancellationToken on shutdown so it can finish cleanly. It is per instance, though: scale to three replicas and your "nightly job" runs three times unless you add a distributed lock or a real scheduler. It has no queue, schedule or retry logic of its own.
questions.asked: The "it runs on every instance" catch is the part that shows production experience.

questions.q: A request to `/me` carries a valid bearer token. What response does it get?
choices: 200, because endpoint routing puts the two middlewares in the right order
401, because authorisation runs while the user is still anonymous
403, because the user is authenticated too late to pass the policy
None: the host refuses to start with the middlewares in this order
questions.why: UseAuthentication is what reads the token and fills `HttpContext.User`. Placed after UseAuthorization, the policy check sees an anonymous user and challenges, so every protected endpoint returns 401 even with a valid token. Nothing re-orders them and nothing fails at startup, which is why this bug survives until the first real request.
questions.asked: A classic misconfiguration; recognising the symptom is more useful than reciting the AuthN/AuthZ definition.

questions.q: What is a claims-based identity?
choices: A role name stored in the database and checked by `[Authorize(Roles)]` attributes
The signature of the JWT, which policies compare against the signing key
The user as a set of claims (key/value statements) that policies evaluate
The username typed into the login form, kept in session state per request
questions.why: A ClaimsPrincipal carries claims such as sub, email and role, issued by whatever authenticated the user. Roles are just one kind of claim. Policy-based authorization (`RequireClaim`, `RequireAssertion`, custom requirements) scales better than scattering role names through attributes.
questions.asked: Leads into policies, which is how real apps express "only the owner or an admin".

questions.q: Why is `IMemoryCache` not enough once you scale out?
choices: It has a fixed limit of 100 MB per process, which fills up quickly once traffic grows
It is not thread-safe, so concurrent requests across instances corrupt it
It can hold only strings, so every instance must serialise its objects
Each instance has its own copy, so entries diverge and eviction does not spread
questions.why: Three instances, three caches, three possibly different answers, and evicting on one does nothing to the others. A distributed cache (Redis, or HybridCache in .NET 9 over one) gives a shared view at the cost of a network hop. IMemoryCache is thread-safe, stores objects and has no fixed size limit unless you set one.
questions.asked: Scaling questions start here; the invalidation part is what interviewers push on.

questions.q: What does `WebApplicationFactory<T>` enable?
choices: Load tests that start many copies of the app and measure its throughput under traffic
Integration tests that boot the real app in memory and send it real requests
Generated client SDKs for the API, built from the endpoints the app maps
Migrations run against a fresh test database before each test class starts
questions.why: It tests routing, model binding, middleware, filters and serialisation together, which a unit test on a handler misses, and lets you swap services. Pair it with a real database in a container (Testcontainers) or SQLite in-memory; Microsoft discourages the EF InMemory provider for this, because it behaves nothing like a relational database.
questions.asked: Shows you test the HTTP surface, not only classes in isolation.

questions.q: How do you configure CORS correctly in ASP.NET Core?
choices: AllowAnyOrigin together with AllowCredentials, so every client can send cookies
An Access-Control-Allow-Origin header added by hand in each controller action
A named policy with explicit origins, applied with UseCors before the endpoints
Nothing: ASP.NET Core allows cross-origin requests by default for JSON endpoints
questions.why: Credentials require an explicit origin, so the CORS policy builder throws if you combine AllowAnyOrigin with AllowCredentials, before any browser gets involved. UseCors placed after the endpoints never sees the preflight. Hand-written headers miss preflight handling, and nothing is allowed cross-origin by default.
questions.asked: Every SPA-plus-API project hits CORS; the interviewer wants the server-side mechanics.

questions.q: What does `services.AddHttpClient<T>()` solve?
choices: Retries on transient failures, which it adds to every client with no configuration
JSON serialisation of request and response bodies, which HttpClient cannot do on its own
Socket exhaustion and stale DNS from creating a client per call or keeping one forever
Authentication headers, which it copies from the incoming request to every call
questions.why: `new HttpClient()` per request leaks sockets in TIME_WAIT; a static instance with default settings never picks up DNS changes. The factory pools and recycles handlers and gives you a place to add resilience handlers. A static client with `SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime` set is also a recommended pattern. Retries are opt-in.
questions.asked: A well-known .NET gotcha that shows whether you have debugged a production networking issue.

questions.q: What changes when ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT is Development instead of Production?
choices: Development turns off DI scope validation and HTTPS, which Production always enables
Production turns off logging, so only Development writes any log output
Development shows the developer exception page with stack traces; Production must not
Nothing at runtime: the variable only picks which appsettings file you edit
questions.why: The environment switches on the developer exception page, user secrets and DI scope validation, and selects `appsettings.{Environment}.json`. A stack trace tells an attacker your framework versions, file paths and sometimes connection strings, so getting this variable wrong in production is a real disclosure risk.
questions.asked: Checks you know what a misconfigured environment variable exposes in production.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to return a 404 from a minimal API endpoint?
choices: Throw a KeyNotFoundException, which the framework maps to a 404 response for you
Return `Results.NotFound()` or `TypedResults.NotFound()` from the handler
Return null, which minimal APIs convert into a 404 Not Found response
Call `context.Abort()` so the client treats the resource as unavailable
questions.why: An unhandled exception becomes a 500, not a 404, and a null return is serialised rather than turned into Not Found. `TypedResults` additionally gives a strongly typed return you can assert on in tests and that feeds OpenAPI metadata correctly. `Abort()` drops the connection.
questions.asked: A quick check of minimal API idioms.

questions.q: You add a field to an entity and the API stops returning existing rows correctly. Where do you look first?
choices: Whether the new field's service is registered correctly in the DI container
Whether a migration was created and applied to that environment's database
Whether the CORS policy lets the new field through to the browser client
Whether the JSON serialiser settings still include properties that are null
questions.why: Model and schema drift is the most common EF Core deployment failure: the code expects a column the database does not have. CORS never filters individual fields, and DI has nothing to do with entity properties. The general lesson: schema changes are deployments, and each environment has its own database state.
questions.asked: A realistic debugging prompt; the interviewer wants a hypothesis, not a guess.

questions.q: What does `MapGroup` give you here?
choices: A separate middleware pipeline that runs only for requests under /api/orders
The two endpoints share the /api/orders prefix and the authorisation requirement
A controller class generated at build time from the handlers mapped in the group
A shared concurrency limit, so only one request in the group runs at a time
questions.why: A route group (.NET 7+) applies a prefix and conventions such as authorisation, filters, tags and rate-limit policies to every endpoint mapped on it. It is endpoint metadata, not a separate middleware branch; for that you would use `app.Map` or `UseWhen`. It keeps a minimal API organised without controllers.
questions.asked: The first thing people ask about minimal APIs is how to organise them; route groups are the answer.

questions.q: What can a minimal API endpoint filter see that a middleware cannot?
choices: The raw request body stream, before anything else in the whole app has read from it
Requests that matched no endpoint at all, such as those that end in 404
The response after it has been sent and the connection has been closed
The handler's bound arguments, such as the deserialised DTO, before it runs
questions.why: Endpoint filters run after model binding, around one handler, so they can validate or transform the actual arguments. Middleware runs earlier on the raw HttpContext and sees every request, including ones that match no endpoint. Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns and filters for per-endpoint logic that needs the typed inputs.
questions.asked: Checks you know the layers in the pipeline and pick the right one for validation or auditing.

questions.q: What does `ValidateOnStart()` add to this registration?
choices: It re-validates the options on every request and rejects requests once they are invalid
It validates appsettings.json against a JSON schema as part of the build
An invalid or missing Smtp setting stops the app at startup, not on first use
It reloads the options automatically whenever the configuration file changes
questions.why: Options are validated lazily by default, when something first reads them, which might be the first password-reset email hours after a deploy. `ValidateOnStart` runs the validation while the host starts, so a bad deploy fails immediately and visibly. It has nothing to do with reloading or per-request checks.
questions.asked: Fail-fast configuration is a production-readiness signal interviewers like to hear.

questions.q: Why prefer the second logging call?
questions.code:
logger.LogInformation($"Order {orderId} shipped to {customerId}");
logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped to {CustomerId}", orderId, customerId);
choices: The first does not compile, because the Log methods reject interpolated strings
The second encrypts the values, so they cannot leak into plain-text log files
It keeps OrderId and CustomerId as queryable fields, and skips formatting when disabled
The first logs asynchronously on another thread, so it can reorder your log messages
questions.why: A message template sends the template and the values separately, so a structured sink stores OrderId as a field you can filter on, and all "Order shipped" events group together. The interpolated version bakes the values into one unique string and is formatted even when Information is disabled. It compiles fine, which is why analysers (CA2254) flag it.
questions.asked: Structured logging is how production issues get found; this is the most common mistake in .NET logging.

questions.q: With these mappings, what does `/health/live` report while the database is down?
choices: Unhealthy, because every registered check runs on every health endpoint
Degraded, because the db check is tagged for a different endpoint and is only partly run
Healthy: its predicate selects no checks, so it only proves the app responds
A 404, because an endpoint whose predicate matches no check is not mapped
questions.why: The predicate chooses which registered checks an endpoint runs. `_ => false` runs none, so liveness reports Healthy whenever the process can answer HTTP, and a database outage does not get the app restarted. The tagged readiness endpoint runs the db check and reports Unhealthy, so traffic is routed away until it recovers.
questions.asked: Mixing liveness and readiness causes restart loops during outages; the tag mechanics are how you avoid it in .NET.

questions.q: The 101st request in a minute to `/search` is rejected. What status does it get with this setup?
choices: 429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After header added automatically
503 Service Unavailable, unless you set RejectionStatusCode to 429
403 Forbidden, because the limiter runs as part of authorisation
None: it waits in a queue until the next window opens, then succeeds
questions.why: The built-in rate limiter (.NET 7+) rejects with 503 by default. Set `options.RejectionStatusCode = 429` and, if you want Retry-After, write it in `OnRejected`. `QueueLimit` defaults to 0, so nothing waits unless you configure a queue. It is independent of authorisation.
questions.asked: A detail you only know from having shipped it; clients that expect 429 break on the default.

questions.q: What is the key difference between output caching (.NET 7+) and the older response caching middleware?
choices: Output caching sets Cache-Control for browsers; response caching stores responses in Redis
Output caching works only for MVC controllers; response caching works only for minimal API endpoints
Output caching stores HTML pages only; response caching stores JSON API responses only
Output caching stores responses on the server by your rules; response caching obeys HTTP headers
questions.why: Response caching follows HTTP caching semantics, so a client sending `Cache-Control: no-cache` bypasses it and your server cache is only as good as the headers. Output caching is a server-side cache configured by policy, with tag-based eviction and resource locking against stampedes, and it ignores client headers. Both work with any endpoint type.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know which cache you are actually configuring, a common source of "caching does nothing" bugs.

questions.q: In `AddJwtBearer`, what does validating the audience (`ValidAudience`) protect against?
choices: A token issued for a different API by the same identity provider being accepted by yours
A token with a forged signature, because the audience value is part of the signing key itself
A token that has expired, because the audience check also covers the token's lifetime
A token replayed from another browser, because the audience binds it to one device
questions.why: One identity provider often issues tokens for many APIs, all signed with the same key. The `aud` claim says which API a token is for, so without the check a token meant for a low-privilege service works against yours. Signature, lifetime and issuer are separate validations (`ValidateIssuerSigningKey`, `ValidateLifetime`, `ValidIssuer`).
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand what each JWT validation parameter is for, not only that defaults exist.

questions.q: Why is this check done in the handler rather than with `[Authorize(Policy = "CanEdit")]`?
choices: Attributes cannot refer to policies that use custom authorisation requirements
The policy needs the loaded document, such as its owner, which only exists here
IAuthorizationService is faster, because it skips the authentication middleware
Forbid() returns 404 here, hiding that the document exists, unlike the attribute
questions.why: Resource-based authorisation passes the resource into the policy so a handler can compare, for example, `doc.OwnerId` with the user's id. An attribute runs before the handler, when the document has not been loaded. Attributes can use custom requirements, and `Forbid()` produces 403 (or the scheme's forbid behaviour), not 404.
questions.asked: "Users can edit only their own records" is in every CRUD app; this is the idiomatic .NET way to express it.

questions.q: In .NET 8+, what does this setup do with an unhandled exception thrown by an endpoint?
choices: Shows the developer exception page in every environment, including Production
Swallows the exception and returns 200 with an empty body to hide the failure
Calls GlobalExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync, which can write a ProblemDetails reply
Logs it and lets it reach Kestrel, which then closes the connection without any response
questions.why: `IExceptionHandler` implementations are called in registration order by the exception handler middleware; one that returns true has handled it. Otherwise the middleware falls back to a ProblemDetails 500 via `AddProblemDetails`. It replaces the hand-written try/catch middleware most codebases used to have, and it never exposes stack traces unless you write them.
questions.asked: The modern answer to "how do you handle errors globally in ASP.NET Core?".

questions.q: What does `[FromKeyedServices("s3")]` inject here (.NET 8+)?
choices: The last IStorage registered, because the key is used only for diagnostics
Every implementation at once, injected together as an `IEnumerable<IStorage>`
A new S3Storage on every request, because keyed services are always transient
The S3Storage registration, chosen by its key rather than registration order
questions.why: Keyed services let several implementations of one interface coexist and be requested by key, without writing a factory or a wrapper interface. The lifetime is whatever you registered, a singleton here. Registration order never matters for a keyed lookup; it is only a set of unkeyed `AddSingleton<IStorage, ...>` calls where the last one wins, which is the ambiguity keys exist to avoid.
questions.asked: A recent DI feature that replaces a lot of hand-rolled factory code.

questions.q: A singleton service copies `HttpContext` from `IHttpContextAccessor` into a field in its constructor. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing: the stored field keeps pointing at whichever request is current at the time
The constructor throws, because a singleton cannot receive the accessor
It keeps one request's HttpContext, which is stale or recycled for later requests
Each request gets its own copy of the singleton, doubling memory use
questions.why: The accessor is safe to inject into a singleton, but only when you read `.HttpContext` at the moment you need it. A stored HttpContext belongs to one request; afterwards its objects are reset and reused, so you read another user's data or get ObjectDisposedException. HttpContext is also not thread-safe, so do not share it across parallel work.
questions.asked: Leads to real data-leak bugs between users; interviewers ask it to find people who have debugged one.

questions.q: Behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS, `Request.Scheme` is http and `RemoteIpAddress` is the proxy's. What fixes it?
choices: UseHttpsRedirection, which rewrites the request scheme to https on every single request
Setting ASPNETCORE_URLS to an https address, so Kestrel reports https
UseHsts, which tells the app that every request arrived over TLS
UseForwardedHeaders, trusting the proxy, to apply X-Forwarded-For and -Proto
questions.why: The proxy passes the original scheme and client IP in X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For; the forwarded headers middleware applies them, but only from proxies you configure as trusted, so clients cannot spoof them. HTTPS redirection alone causes a redirect loop here, because every request looks like http. HSTS only sets a browser header.
questions.asked: Every containerised deployment sits behind a proxy; wrong scheme and IP break redirects, cookies and rate limiting.

questions.q: In a new .NET 9 Web API project, what generates the OpenAPI document?
choices: Swashbuckle's AddSwaggerGen, which the template still includes by default
NSwag, which is compiled into ASP.NET Core itself starting with .NET 9
Nothing: OpenAPI support was removed from ASP.NET Core in .NET 9
Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, via AddOpenApi and MapOpenApi
questions.why: From .NET 9 the templates use the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi package: `AddOpenApi()` registers generation and `MapOpenApi()` serves the JSON document. Swashbuckle was removed from the templates, though it still works if you add it. A UI (Swagger UI or Scalar) is a separate choice.
questions.asked: A currency check; tutorials written before .NET 9 still show Swashbuckle.

questions.q: In .NET 8+, a minimal API endpoint binds `[FromForm]` data and the app uses antiforgery. A POST arrives without a token. What happens?
choices: It succeeds, because minimal API endpoints never validate antiforgery tokens
It is rejected, because form-binding endpoints validate the token automatically
It succeeds, provided that the request also carries a valid authentication cookie
It is redirected to the login page, where the client can fetch a fresh token
questions.why: With `AddAntiforgery()` and `UseAntiforgery()`, minimal API endpoints that bind form data require a valid token and reject the request (400) without one; `DisableAntiforgery()` opts an endpoint out. The auth cookie is exactly what a cross-site form would ride on, so it proves nothing. JSON APIs using bearer tokens do not need this.
questions.asked: Checks you know where CSRF protection is automatic in .NET and where it is not.

questions.q: By default, where does each parameter of this minimal API handler bind from?
questions.code:
app.MapPost("/orders/{id:int}",
    (int id, OrderDto body, IOrderService svc, int? page) => Results.Ok());
choices: id from the route, body from JSON, svc from DI, page from the query string
id and page from the query string, body from the form, svc from the route
id from the route, body from the query string, svc and page from headers
All four from the JSON body, matched to its properties by each parameter name
questions.why: Minimal APIs infer sources: a name in the route template binds from the route, a registered service from DI, a complex type from the JSON body, and remaining simple types from the query string. Use `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader]`, `[FromServices]` or `[FromForm]` when the inference is not what you want.
questions.asked: Binding surprises cause most "my parameter is null" questions; knowing the rules prevents them.

questions.q: A minimal API returns `new { Status = OrderStatus.Shipped }` and the React client receives `{"status": 2}`. Why, and what is the idiomatic fix?
choices: System.Text.Json writes enums as numbers by default; add `JsonStringEnumConverter` to the JSON options
Web defaults camel-cased the property and dropped its enum type; decorate it with `[JsonPropertyName]`
The anonymous type boxed the enum to an int; return a record with a typed `OrderStatus` property instead
The client sent `Accept: application/json` without a schema; add OpenAPI so it can map the number back
questions.why: System.Text.Json serialises an enum as its underlying integer unless a converter says otherwise; `builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o => o.SerializerOptions.Converters.Add(new JsonStringEnumConverter()))` (or `AddJsonOptions` for controllers) makes it write and accept "Shipped". Camel-casing only touches the property name, an anonymous type keeps the enum's type, and OpenAPI describes output rather than changing it. Numbers also break the moment someone reorders the enum.
questions.asked: A first-week bug on every .NET-plus-React team; the interviewer wants the mechanism and the one-line fix.
